title: Build an AI Analyst You Can Trust

slides.title: Build an AI Analyst You Can Trust
slides.body: Khaled Zaky
slides.qr: Everything from tonight, including a no-code track
slides.notes: Doors: leave this up while people sit. At 6:15, Cmd+2 for the brief. Say nothing for three seconds. "One of the facts on this page is made up. Tonight is about which person you want to be: the one who sends that, or the one who catches it." Then Cmd+1.

slides.title: I'm Khaled.
slides.body:
I lead AI Governance and Evaluations Platform Engineering at RBC Borealis.
Before that, I built and led the bank's agentic AI platform. Before that, I shipped passkeys and MFA for AWS sign-in.
I think governance belongs inside the system from day one. Tonight you'll watch me build it in.
slides.notes: Under a minute. RBC Borealis, the agentic platform, passkeys and MFA at AWS, and you teach PM and AI here at BrainStation. Land it on: governance belongs inside the system from day one, and tonight you'll watch me build it in.

slides.title: An AI can draft it in seconds. Would you sign it?
slides.body:
Anyone here can get an AI to write a brief or a deck in under a minute.
Putting your name on it still takes as long as it always did, and a wrong number lands on whoever forwarded it.
The people who get handed real work are the ones whose AI output can be checked.
slides.notes: Cast the room: PM, eng lead, or an exec who wants an assistant to hand real work to. Same move for all of you: you're hiring a teammate and deciding whether to trust it.

slides.title: Tonight
slides.notes: Fifteen seconds. Watch it build, catch it, your turn, what to keep. The red tags are where I go live.

slides.title: Do we fix substitutions next quarter?
slides.body:
You order parsley. We're out, so we send cilantro, and customers hate it.
We have 90 days of complaints in one file and a decision to make.
Someone would normally spend half a day reading all of it. Let's watch a machine do it instead.
slides.notes: Parsley, cilantro, customers hate it. Ninety days of complaints and a decision. "Normally somebody spends half a day reading this. Let's watch a machine do it." Then → to LIVE.

slides.title: I built this agent with Claude Code.
slides.body: Claude writes. Code checks.
slides.notes: Twenty-five seconds, walk it top to bottom. "I built this agent before tonight, with Claude Code. Here's the whole system. Two inputs: the feedback file, and a contract plus three step prompts. In the middle, Claude runs in a loop: it picks a tool, reads the file or searches the web, looks at what came back, and goes again until it decides the brief is done. Out comes a brief where every claim carries its source and the exact sentence it came from. Then the bottom half is plain code, no model: the gate. Claude writes. Code checks." Then →.

slides.title: One level down: the loop
slides.body: About 40 lines in freshcart_agent/agent.py. Tonight it replays a run I set up, so it runs the same way every time. The check you'll watch me build runs for real.
slides.notes: Twenty seconds. Point, don't read. "One level down, this is the loop. Send Claude the contract, the two tools and the conversation so far. If it asks for a tool, run it and hand the result back. If it doesn't, it's done. About forty lines. Tonight it replays a run I set up, so it runs the same way every time and the venue wifi can't break it. The check runs for real, and you'll watch me build it." Then →.

slides.title: The contract is what makes it checkable.
slides.body: Every claim names its source and the exact sentence behind it. All of it is on GitHub: github.com/kzaky/freshcart-agent
slides.qr: The repo, every prompt, and the no-code track
slides.notes: Twenty seconds. "And this is what makes it checkable. The contract says every web claim records the exact sentence it came from, and that sentence will be checked. So every claim comes out like this: the claim, the source, the quote. Hold on to that quote field; it's what we check in part two. All of it is on GitHub: the agent, the prompts, the gate, and the prompt I gave Claude Code to start it. The QR gets you there, and I'll show it again at the end." Then → to LIVE.

slides.title: make demo
slides.body: The agent reads 182 pieces of feedback and writes the brief. A replay: the same run every time.
slides.notes: Ctrl+→, tab 1, make demo. It prints in about six seconds: let it finish, scroll up, walk the phases (182 pieces of feedback, the four themes, the two searches, the brief). The banner says REPLAY; own it. "A run like this costs about eight cents and takes about twenty seconds." Ctrl+←, Cmd+2, scroll the brief, don't point at 62%. Bait: "You could have pasted this into a chatbot. You're right." Cmd+1, then →. Dead? ↓ output, ↓ brief.

slides.title: Each of these has a source. One of them is invented.
slides.body:
• Substitution complaints account for 68 of 182 feedback items in the last 90 days.
• 41% of shoppers reduced order frequency after poor substitutions.
• InstaFresh lets customers pre-approve a substitute per item.
• 62% of FreshCart users churn after a single bad substitution.
slides.notes: Sixty seconds. Take two or three guesses out loud and confirm none of them. "Catching this is literally my job, and I read straight past it too. So let's build something that checks every line."

slides.title: Tonight
slides.notes: Two seconds. "Part two. Now we catch it, live."

slides.title: Every fact carries the exact sentence it came from.
slides.body: Then something goes back to the source and checks that the sentence is really there.
slides.notes: Say it slowly, it's the most valuable sentence of the night: every fact carries the exact sentence it came from, and something goes back and checks it's really there. Then → to LIVE.

slides.title: make gate
slides.body: Claude Code writes the check, then we run it.

fallback.title: The brief, with the failed claim flagged

slides.notes: Ctrl+→, tab 2, Cmd+V the prompt (on the clipboard from pre-flight), Enter. Keep talking: "I described what I want checked in English, and it's writing the code." If it offers to run the gate, say no. Stall past 90s: tab 1, \cp ../freshcart_agent/gate.py freshcart_agent/gate.py. Tab 1, make gate. Pass, pass, pass. Hold the RED four seconds. Ctrl+←, then →. Dead? ↓ RED run, ↓ flagged brief.

slides.title: It stretched a real finding into a better story.

cols.label: What the brief said
cols.text: 62% of FreshCart users churn after a single bad substitution.

cols.label: What the report says
cols.text: 41% of shoppers reduced order frequency after poor substitutions.

slides.notes: "The report never says sixty-two, and it never says anyone left. The real number is forty-one percent, and it's about ordering less often." Then the disclosure: "Full disclosure: this is a replay of a run I set up, and I planted this claim so it fails the same way every time. The gate didn't know. It ran for real, just now." Empathy, slowly: your VP repeats it, and three months later the honest answer is nowhere. "I didn't catch it. The check did." Then → to LIVE.

slides.title: make fix, make gate
slides.body: Drop the claim that failed, then check again.
slides.notes: Ctrl+→, tab 1, make fix, then make gate. GREEN. "Same agent. Now it's earned the decision." "The gate, and the prompt I just pasted, are in the repo's workshop folder." Ctrl+←, Cmd+3, Cmd+R: the evidence pack. "It left a receipt, and that receipt is what separates a weekend project from something a bank will run." Cmd+1, then →. Dead? ↓ GREEN, ↓ evidence pack.

slides.title: Tonight
slides.notes: Two seconds. "Part three is yours."

slides.title: Now you catch it.
slides.body: It works on a phone. If the wifi is slow, wherever you get to is fine.
slides.notes: Thirty seconds to scan. "Tap Try the check in 2 minutes, right under the rule near the top." The QR is on the handout too. Wherever they get to is fine.

slides.title: Four steps, one chat
slides.body:
• Open claude.ai and start a new chat. It's free and there's nothing to install.
• Copy the contract from the site and paste it as your first message.
• Paste the sample brief, which has one fabricated number hiding in it.
• Paste the verifier, then watch what your Claude does with each claim.
slides.notes: About seven minutes. Walk the room. Wifi dies: "Screens down, everyone watch mine," Cmd+5 for your own claude.ai tab and run the three pastes.

slides.title: Hands up if your Claude passed everything.
slides.body:
Same prompt and same brief, and this room got three verdicts: caught it, couldn't reach the source, or made a sentence up.
A chat can't hold the source, so the check that decides has to be code that does.
slides.notes: Hands up if it passed everything. Then hands up if it failed everything. Three verdicts from one prompt: caught it, couldn't reach the source, or made a sentence up. A chat can't hold the source, so the check that decides is code, about sixty lines of Python and not a second AI.

slides.title: Tonight
slides.notes: Two seconds. "Last part. No more live demos, just what to keep."

slides.title: Three jobs in this room

cols.label: Product manager
cols.text: Your brief survives the review. When a VP asks where a number came from, you hand over the evidence pack.

cols.label: Engineering lead
cols.text: Run it as a test on every commit. A prompt tweak that drops groundedness fails the build before anyone sees it.

cols.label: Executive
cols.text: You can sign without re-reading every number, because you're trusting a check you can audit.

slides.notes: Sixty seconds each at most. PM: the evidence pack keeps your brief alive in review. Eng lead: run it as a test on every commit. Exec: you sign a check you can audit, not an AI you have to trust.

slides.title: Three names for the same code

cols.label: Engineering
cols.text: An eval. Did it do the job?

cols.label: Risk
cols.text: A guardrail. Did it avoid harm?

cols.label: Regulators
cols.text: Governance. Can you prove it to someone who wasn't in the room?

slides.notes: Forty-five seconds. Engineers say eval, risk says guardrail, regulators say governance. Same code, three rooms, so learn to say all three.

slides.title: The four numbers you already saw
slides.body:
• Groundedness: 3 of 4 on the first run, 3 of 3 after the fix
• Completion: 5 of 5 brief sections present
• Cost: about 8 cents a run (estimated)
• Latency: about 19 seconds a run (estimated)
slides.notes: Thirty seconds. Point, don't re-explain: they were on screen when the gate passed. Groundedness is the one almost nobody tracks, and the one that ends careers. Cost and latency are estimates for a run like this; tonight's was a replay.

slides.title: Ask again tomorrow and you get a different answer.
slides.body:
Test regular software once and it stays tested. A model can answer the same question two different ways.
So the check runs on every run, and it never comes off.
slides.notes: Forty-five seconds. Same question tomorrow, different answer, so the check runs every time and never comes off. Running long? Skip to 21.

slides.title: Four ways a brief goes wrong
slides.body:
• Fabrication: a fact with no source at all
• Drift: a real source, bent to a number it never said (tonight's 62%)
• Omission: the counter-evidence quietly goes missing
• Silent regression: a model update breaks what works today
slides.notes: "What I showed you is one check." Four shapes, none needing a model that's trying to lie. Drift is tonight's 62%, and the dangerous one because it survives a careful read. You can't check for a failure you haven't named.

slides.title: Let a model judge, carefully
slides.body:
• It prefers longer answers
• It likes its own phrasing best
• It can make the same mistake the writer made
• Use it to rank and triage, and keep the gate itself in code
slides.notes: Where code can't judge tone or usefulness, a model can, carefully: it has a thumb on the scale. Rank and triage with it, calibrate it against people, and keep the gate in code.

slides.title: What even a perfect gate misses
slides.body:
• A real source bent to the wrong conclusion
• Counter-evidence nobody cited
• Bad reasoning built on sound facts
• So it takes a suite, and a human still signs
slides.notes: Slow down, even at your pace. The honesty peak. It catches a made-up citation, not a real source bent to the wrong conclusion. So it takes a suite, and a human still signs. The gate removes the failure you're worst at, the confident, well-sourced, wrong number.

slides.title: Four ways to check an answer
slides.body: Match the method to the question. The full map is at khaledzaky.com/trust/evals.

cols.label: Code
cols.text: Exact, cheap and impossible to argue with. It can't judge tone.

cols.label: Reference answer
cols.text: A clear signal when a known-good answer exists. Useless when one doesn't.

cols.label: Model as judge
cols.text: Handles nuance at scale. Comes with biases you have to design around.

cols.label: Human review
cols.text: The ground truth. Too slow for every run, so use it to calibrate the others.

slides.notes: One minute. Code, a reference answer, a model as judge, a human. Each fails somewhere different. The full map is the evals link in the chat.

slides.title: Four questions before AI output reaches a real decision
slides.body:
• Can every fact name its source?
• Does something check that source automatically, or only a human on a good day?
• When the check fails, does it block the document, or warn and get ignored?
• Could you show someone the receipt six months from now?
slides.notes: Two minutes. The only thing they write down, so read them slowly and give them time. It's the checklist on their seat and on the site.

slides.title: The nine controls behind tonight
slides.body: Tools change every quarter. These controls stay the same.

cols.label: What goes in
cols.text: Source of record, a grounding contract, a scope boundary

cols.label: What comes out
cols.text: A structured artifact, a groundedness check, a gate that fails closed

cols.label: What proves it
cols.text: The evidence pack, run metrics, a regression set

slides.notes: Thirty seconds. What goes in, what comes out, what proves it. Every module on the site says which ones it implements.

slides.title: Rebuild it yourself

cols.label: No-code track
cols.text: claude.ai and seven copy-paste prompts, in order. Save them as a Claude Project or skill to reuse. No install, no API key. You do the checking.

cols.label: Builder track
cols.text: Claude Code and the repo at github.com/kzaky/freshcart-agent: the agent, the gate, and the prompt I started it from.

slides.notes: Thirty seconds. No-code: claude.ai and seven prompts, no install, no API key; save them as a Project or skill. In a chat, you're the checker. Builder: say the URL out loud, "github dot com slash kzaky slash freshcart-agent. The prompt I gave Claude Code to start this agent is in there too."

slides.title: These slides came from the same generator as the FreshCart deck.
slides.body:
Same code. I didn't make an exception for myself.
The agent read 182 pieces of feedback, ranked the problems, pulled the evidence, wrote the recommendation, built a deck and left a receipt for every claim. A run like that costs about 8 cents.
slides.notes: "The slides I taught with tonight came out of the same generator that turned the approved brief into a leadership deck. Same code." Press ↓ to show that deck for five seconds, ↑ to hide it. Then the recap: 182 pieces of feedback, about eight cents a run.

fallback.title: The leadership deck, from the same generator

slides.title: You already knew how to make the trick.
slides.body:
Now you're the person who can be trusted with it.
Every fact carries the sentence it came from, and something goes and checks.
slides.qr: The site, the checklist and the evals map
slides.notes: "You're walking out as the person who can be trusted with it." The three links are already in the chat: the site, the checklist, the evals map. "Thank you. Questions?"

slides.title: Questions
slides.body: The checklist and the evals map are both linked from the site.
slides.notes: Hard stop at 7:20. Leave the QR up. Likely questions: isn't the checker just another AI, isn't this rigged (you planted it and said so; the replay file in the repo says it's engineered), what else would you run in production, I can't code.
